body: {"total":6,"records":[{"title":"A structured electronic referral form for specialist outpatient referrals and the proportion of referrals returned for missing information","authors":"Okwuosa-Brandt L, Hollis-Nakamura E, Sepulveda-Grant R","year":2018,"venue":"Journal of Referral and Access Management","doi":"10.5555/jram.2018.0204","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"Two specialist services replaced free-text referral letters with an electronic form containing required fields for the most common referral reasons. We compared the 12 months before and after the change. Referrals returned to family practices for missing information fell from 19 percent to 7 percent, and the median time from receipt to a triage decision fell from 8 to 4 working days. The number of referrals received did not change. The comparison was uncontrolled, a new triage coordinator started in the same month, and the authors did not measure the time family practices spent completing the form."},{"title":"Mandatory-field referral templates and triage time: a stepped introduction across 48 family practices","authors":"Lindqvist-Adeyemi K, Carvalho-Stroud P, Mensah-Fairbairn A","year":2022,"venue":"Health Services Access Review","doi":"10.5555/hsar.2022.0319","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"A mandatory-field referral template was introduced to 48 family practices in four steps over eight months, in a random order of practice groups. Across 11,260 referrals there was no difference in the time from receipt to triage decision between periods with and without the template (adjusted difference 0.3 days, 95 percent CI -0.6 to 1.2). Returned referrals fell only in practices that used the template for more than half of their referrals. Overall, 38 percent of referrals bypassed the required fields by attaching a free-text letter. Practices reported that the template took longer to complete than a letter."},{"title":"Tick boxes and workarounds: family physicians' views of structured specialist referral templates","authors":"Achebe-Morrow T, Varga-Hendricks S","year":2020,"venue":"Primary Care Organisation Studies","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We spoke with 24 family physicians and 11 practice staff in three regions about structured referral templates. Participants valued templates that pulled test results automatically and disliked required fields that repeated information already in the letter. Many described the templates as moving the specialist service's work into the practice without extra time. Several admitted attaching a letter to avoid required fields, especially for complex patients. Participants wanted to know what happened to returned referrals. The sample was drawn from practices that had volunteered for a regional template group."},{"title":"Required faecal immunochemical test results in suspected lower gastrointestinal cancer referrals: an interrupted time series","authors":"Petrossian-Kaye D, Obi-Lindgren M","year":2023,"venue":"Journal of Referral and Access Management","doi":"10.5555/jram.2023.0077","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"A regional referral service made a faecal immunochemical test result a required field for urgent lower gastrointestinal referrals. In an interrupted time series over 30 months, the proportion of urgent referrals with a test result rose from 54 percent to 91 percent. Returned referrals rose in the first three months after the change and returned to the previous level by six months. Time to colonoscopy for urgent referrals did not change. Practices without access to rapid test kits returned the most referrals, and the authors warn that required fields can delay referrals from those practices."},{"title":"Value stream mapping of a central referral intake: waste in handoffs and rework","authors":"Grieve-Otieno B, Salazar-Whitby J","year":2016,"venue":"Lean Health Operations","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"A central referral intake serving six specialties mapped its value stream with nurses, clerks and referring practices. Staff spent about 60 percent of triage nurse time on rework: chasing missing information, re-keying faxed letters and answering practice queries about returned referrals. After a redesign that added a single returned-referral queue and a fixed daily triage time, the median lead time from receipt to triage fell from 12 to 6 working days over four months. No referral template was introduced. The evaluation was a before-after comparison without a control and without follow-up beyond four months."},{"title":"Referral forms and guidelines for specialist referral: a systematic review of effects on referral quality and access","authors":"Harcourt-Ibeh N, Tanaka-Poulsen R, Oduya-Ferris C, Kamara-Lind J","year":2021,"venue":"Health Services Access Review","doi":"10.5555/hsar.2021.0142","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We included 21 studies of structured referral forms or referral guidelines for specialist outpatient services. Thirteen reported better referral quality, usually more complete information, with structured forms. Effects on waiting times were measured in seven studies and were inconsistent: three reported shorter times and four found no change. Only two studies measured the time family practices spent on referrals. Most studies were uncontrolled before-after comparisons, and definitions of referral quality varied. The authors conclude that structured forms improve completeness but that effects on access remain uncertain."}]}
